source.title: Learn From All: Erasing Attention Consistency for Noisy Label Facial Expression Recognition
source.authors: Yuhang Zhang; Chengrui Wang; Xu Ling; Wei-Hong Deng

record.tranche_reason: Tests performance under several levels of label noise on FER datasets, using a different method and evaluation measure from the claim. It does not test the full random-label or unstructured-input settings.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports test accuracy for Baseline, SCN, RUL and EAC on three datasets at 10%, 20% and 30% label noise. The paper does not report training error for these conditions. Its statements and Figure 5 about memorizing noisy samples are qualitative and do not establish fitting completely random labels or perfect training accuracy.
record.test_reason: The baseline provides evidence on V4 in facial expression recognition: Section 4.7 reports losses near zero for nearly all clean and noisy training samples at 30% corruption, while baseline test accuracy declines across 10%, 20% and 30% corruption. The record incorrectly dismisses the training-loss evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that EAC suppresses noisy-label memorization, improves noisy-label FER performance, and extends to classification with many classes. Their baseline also memorizes nearly all noisy samples in the reported 30%-noise experiment.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a proposed attention-consistency training method on partially noisy-label datasets; it does not use the original random-label memorization experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and label-noise percentage affect reported test accuracy; the paper also reports different outcomes across training methods.

fits_no_version.finding: EAC improves test accuracy and maintains separation between clean and noisy training losses after 60 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Erasing attention consistency suppresses noisy-label memorization while preserving useful classification features.

fits_no_version.finding: SCN can predict a noisy training label on an original image while predicting its latent true label after flipping.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noisy-label memorization can depend on image orientation and localized features.

record.problems: No training accuracy or training error is reported for the noisy-label experiments, so the results cannot establish whether the models fit the noisy training labels. Only 10%, 20% and 30% noise are reported in Table 1; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows retained because the reported Table 1 measure is test accuracy and does not establish the training-fit behavior named by V4. Qualitative claims about memorization and Figure 5 likewise do not report a measure of fitting completely random labels or perfect training accuracy.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes.
Comparative training time and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit across corruption levels; degradation through complete corruption toward chance. Near-zero baseline training losses are reported only at 30% corruption.
Random-label fitting under weight decay, dropout and augmentation, and true-label generalization after removing these regularizers.
Learning order for clean versus noisy labels. Figure 5 shows endpoint loss distributions, not learning trajectories.

missing.what: Restore the baseline training-loss finding wrongly excluded by rows_left_out: at 30% noise on RAF-DB, nearly all clean and noisy samples have classification loss near zero after 60 epochs. This is qualitative evidence of near-complete training fit, although no exact training-error percentage is supplied.
Record baseline RAF-DB test accuracy across noise levels, paired with the training-fit evidence: 81.01%, 77.98% and 75.50% at 10%, 20% and 30% corruption.

Additional baseline test-degradation results omitted from the record's coverage: MobileNet accuracy is 83.31%, 77.80%, 70.60%, 62.48%; ResNet-50 accuracy is 88.75%, 83.44%, 79.11%, 71.67%, at 0%, 10%, 20%, 30% corruption respectively. Training fit is not established for these backbones.

record.verdict_notes: EAC is a purpose-built mitigation with an added consistency objective; its reduced memorization does not challenge the claims about standard training. Endpoint loss distributions do not establish V6. No numerical training-error rate should be inferred from Figure 5.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, test error at chance, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters are not tested.
Training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases are not reported.
Shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

Test accuracy is reported at 10%, 20% and 30% noise, but training error is not reported; noise levels of none and all are not evaluated in Table 1, and the paper does not establish steady degradation across the full range or that the remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.
The study does not test whether weight decay, dropout or data augmentation permit fitting random labels, or whether removing them changes generalization on true labels.
The study does not measure learning order over training for real versus noisy or random labels.

relationships.condition: Baseline ResNet-18 on RAF-DB with 30% label noise, with test degradation measured over 10–30% noise
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; no extracted row ids exist. Section 4.7 reports nearly all training losses near zero at 30% noise; Table 1 baseline test accuracy falls from 81.01% to 77.98% to 75.50% as corruption increases.
relationships.display_finding: Nearly all training losses approached zero at 30% noise, while test accuracy declined from 81.01% to 77.98% to 75.50% across increasing corruption levels.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
